passage: It was festival week and the hostel corridor thumped with drums until midnight, with an exam in five days. Sarika sat on her bed with her grandmother's small book of verses, reading the same page for the third time. Something in one line made her stop. For a week she got up early, in the little quiet before the drums, and read a verse and sat still. It comforted her. But she noticed how tempting it was to copy an answer down whole and stop asking. On Saturday she took the book to Irawati Tai, the warden's elderly aunt who ran a study circle. "What do you think this line means?" asked Irawati Tai, instead of explaining. Sarika hesitated. "I'm not sure. Part of it makes me uneasy." "Good," said Irawati Tai. "Bring that too."

qa.q: How many days were left before Sarika's exam?
How did Sarika feel about turning to the verses?
qa.a: Comforted by them, but wary of how tempting it was to copy an answer down whole and stop asking.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that was wise?
qa.a: She let the verses comfort her and also took them to Irawati Tai to discuss, including the parts that made her uneasy.

qa.q: How might Irawati Tai see Sarika's unease with the line?
qa.a: As a useful sign of real thinking, since Irawati Tai said "Good" and asked her to bring that too.

grounding: The protagonist turns to a book of verses for meaning and lets it comfort her while questioning and discussing it with others, not taking a ready-made answer.

passage:
Sudha beti, you're reading that philosophy book every night now, yes? Good. Let your Irfan nana tell you about when I was twenty and lost. My father had died, I'd failed my exams, and nothing made sense. I started going to a Sufi poetry circle on Thursdays, in an old house near the dargah. We read Rumi and Bulleh Shah and argued about them over tea.

The poems comforted me. They also annoyed me, questioned me, kept me awake. The old teacher never gave answers. He only said, "What do you think it means?"

There was another group nearby with a man who had an answer for everything. My friend Salim went there. He became very sure, very fast, and stopped asking anything at all.

I stayed with the questions. I still have them. They've been better company than certainty.

qa.q: On which day did the Sufi poetry circle meet?
How did young Irfan feel when he started going to the poetry circle?
qa.a: Young Irfan felt lost and grieving after his father's death and failed exams, searching for meaning.

qa.q: What choice inside the story made a difference between Irfan and Salim?
qa.a: Irfan chose the circle that questioned and discussed, while Salim chose a group with ready answers and stopped asking questions.

qa.q: How might the old teacher have seen young Irfan's questions?
qa.a: The teacher seemed to welcome them, since he always turned questions back to Irfan instead of giving answers.

grounding: The elder's story shows a young man turning to a tradition for meaning, letting it both comfort and challenge him, and discussing it with others.

passage:
Night shifts at the call centre in Gurugram left Tanuja with odd hours and an empty head. At 4 am, between calls, she started reading a small book of Buddhist teachings a colleague had lent her. The lines about impermanence made her cry in the washroom once. Another line annoyed her so much she argued with it in the margin.

On Sundays she met Minakshi, an old school friend, at a tea stall, and they talked through the chapters. Minakshi was Christian and brought her own questions; they compared.

In March a man at a weekend meditation session offered Tanuja a place in his group. "You don't need other books," he said. "I will tell you what everything means."

She felt tempted, tired as she was. It would be so easy. Then she thought of her messy margins and the Sunday arguments. She thanked him, and kept her book.

qa.q: What did Tanuja start reading at 4 am?
qa.a: Tanuja started reading a small book of Buddhist teachings a colleague had lent her.

qa.q: Why was Tanuja tempted by the man's offer?
qa.a: Tanuja felt tired and tempted by the ease of having someone tell her what everything meant.

qa.q: Why was keeping her book and Sunday talks the wiser choice?
qa.a: They let the teachings comfort and challenge her and kept her thinking, while the ready-made answers would have spared her from thinking.

qa.q: How might Minakshi see their Sunday conversations?
qa.a: Minakshi seems to enjoy them as an exchange of questions between two faiths, not a contest.

grounding: The story shows a young woman turning to a tradition for meaning, letting it challenge and comfort her, discussing with others and refusing ready-made answers.
